A configuration of N numbered atoms is the point x = (x_1, y_1, z_1, ..., x_N, y_N, z_N) in R^{3N}; the film's molecule has N = 5 atoms (C, C, O, N, H; bonds C-C, C-O, C-N, O-H), so a configuration is a point of R^15.

The film's potential energy U is a sum of harmonic springs, U = sum over all atom pairs of (1/2) k (d_ij - d_ij^rest)^2, with a stiff spring constant on bonded pairs and a weak one on all other pairs, rest lengths taken from the rest geometry; it depends only on interatomic distances.
With SE(3) acting on configurations by x_i -> R x_i + a on every atom (R in SO(3), a in R^3), a potential that depends only on interatomic distances satisfies U(g . x) = U(x) for every g in SE(3).
Rotating every atom about the centre of the molecule instead of the origin is the same symmetry statement, because the two rotations differ by a translation, which is itself a symmetry.
The orbit of x is SE(3) . x; U is constant on orbits and therefore defines a function on the quotient M = R^{3N}/SE(3) (shape space), whose points [x] are orbits.
SE(3) is six-dimensional and acts freely on configurations whose atoms are not all collinear; on a collinear configuration the rotations about the common line fix it.
Away from collinear configurations, M = R^{3N}/SE(3) is a smooth manifold of dimension 3N - 6, which is 9 for N = 5.
The spring energy is also invariant under reflections, but the quotient is taken by SE(3) only, so a configuration and its mirror image are in general different points of M.
A tangent vector at x is one 3-vector per atom; the tangent space T_x R^{3N} is a copy of R^{3N}.

The vertical space at x is V_x = {(v + omega x (x_i - c))_i : v, omega in R^3}, the tangent space of the orbit SE(3) . x; for non-collinear x it is six-dimensional, the image of the Lie algebra se(3).
Vertical vectors change neither the energy nor the shape (they are tangent to the orbit).

For any complement H_x of V_x, T_x R^{3N} = V_x (+) H_x with dim H_x = 3N - 6 (15 = 6 + 9 for N = 5), and the derivative of the projection x -> [x] maps H_x isomorphically onto the tangent space of M at [x].
The complement H_x is not unique; a smooth choice of horizontal complements is a connection.

On the torus T^2 with coordinates (theta, phi) and an energy depending only on theta, the circle group S^1 = U(1) acts by phi -> phi + const, preserves the energy, acts freely, and the quotient T^2/S^1 is the circle of theta values: T^2 -> S^1, (theta, phi) -> theta, is a principal U(1)-bundle with the small circles as fibres.
The torus bundle T^2 -> S^1 is trivial (it is the product S^1 x S^1); every principal U(1)-bundle over a circle is trivial.
The Hopf fibration S^1 -> S^3 -> S^2 is a principal U(1)-bundle whose fibres are great circles of S^3, whose base is the 2-sphere, and which has no global section, so it is not a product.

In any fibre bundle the vertical space at p is the tangent space of the fibre through p, equal to the kernel of the derivative of the projection; a horizontal space is any complement, and the derivative of the projection maps it isomorphically onto the tangent space of the base.

In the cut-open torus (theta to the right, phi upwards) the film's connection has horizontal slope dphi/dtheta = lambda c(theta) with c(theta) = 0.8 sin(theta); invariance under the shift of phi forces the slope to be independent of phi.

The horizontal lift through (theta_s, phi_s) for c(theta) = 0.8 sin(theta) is phi(theta) = phi_s + 0.8 lambda (cos(theta_s) - cos(theta)); following lifts from one fibre to another defines parallel transport between fibres.

A connection is equivalently its connection one-form A, which sends each tangent vector to its vertical part; on the torus A = dphi - lambda c(theta) dtheta, with A(d/dphi) = 1 and horizontal space ker A.

If the total space carries a metric invariant under the structure group, H_p = V_p^perp (orthogonal complement of the vertical space) is a connection; for the flat metric dtheta^2 + dphi^2 on the cut-open torus this is the untilted connection lambda = 0.
The metric induced on a torus of revolution in R^3, (R + r cos phi)^2 dtheta^2 + r^2 dphi^2, is not invariant under shifts of phi.
The kinetic-energy metric <u, v>_x = sum_i m_i u_i . v_i on R^{3N} is invariant under rigid motions; with u = v equal to the velocity it is twice the kinetic energy.

With the kinetic-energy metric, u is orthogonal to all translations iff sum_i m_i u_i = 0 (zero total linear momentum), and orthogonal to all rotations iff sum_i m_i (x_i - c) x u_i = 0 with c the centre of mass (zero total angular momentum); H_x = V_x^perp defines the mechanical connection.
An isolated system that starts with zero total linear and angular momentum keeps zero momentum, so all its motions are horizontal for the mechanical connection.
A field of lines (rank-one distribution) is always integrable; the horizontal lifts of the film's torus connection (c = 0.8 sin theta) close up into circles tangent to H everywhere.
The curvature of a connection is a two-form on the base (with values in the Lie algebra); on a one-dimensional base every two-form vanishes, so every connection on a bundle over a circle is flat.

For c(theta) = 0.8 sin(theta) + mu on the torus, the connection is flat, and the horizontal lift after one full turn of the base returns to its fibre shifted by lambda times the integral of c over [0, 2 pi], which is 2 pi lambda mu; it closes up exactly when lambda mu is an integer, and the holonomy vanishes for mu = 0.
Curvature controls holonomy only around loops that bound a region (contractible loops); the base circle of the torus bundle is not contractible in the base.
Electromagnetism is a U(1) gauge theory: the electromagnetic potential is a connection on a U(1)-bundle and the field strength F = dA is its curvature.

In the Aharonov-Bohm effect charged particles move where the magnetic field vanishes (a flat connection) yet acquire a relative phase q Phi / hbar around a solenoid enclosing flux Phi: holonomy of a flat connection around a non-contractible loop.

On the bundle R^2 x R -> R^2 with coordinates (x, y | z), the connection A = dz - (lambda/2)(x dy - y dx) has horizontal plane at (x, y) spanned by e_1 = (1, 0, -lambda y/2) and e_2 = (0, 1, lambda x/2), independent of z, with slope lambda r / 2 at distance r from the origin.
For lambda = 0 the horizontal planes are tangent to the sheets z = const, so the distribution is integrable and the connection flat.

Frobenius: the plane field ker A of a nowhere-vanishing one-form A on a 3-manifold has an integral surface through every point iff A ^ dA = 0; for A = dz - (lambda/2)(x dy - y dx), A ^ dA = -lambda dz ^ dx ^ dy, nonzero for lambda != 0.

Along a horizontal lift of the plane bundle dz = (lambda/2)(x dy - y dx), so by Green's theorem the lift of a closed loop gamma ends at height z_0 + lambda times the signed area enclosed by gamma (counterclockwise positive), independent of the loop's shape, speed and starting height.
For the unit circle and lambda = 0.5 the holonomy of the plane bundle is 0.5 pi, approximately 1.57.
The discrete lift z_{k+1} = z_k + (lambda/2)(x_k y_{k+1} - y_k x_{k+1}) along a closed polygon adds up to exactly lambda times the polygon's (shoelace) area.

For horizontal vectors u, v and the small base parallelogram with sides eps u, eps v, the vertical displacement of its horizontal lift is eps^2 Omega(u, v) + O(eps^3); Omega is bilinear and antisymmetric, hence a two-form with values in the vertical directions.
For the tilted-tile connection |Omega| = lambda at every point; dA = -lambda dx ^ dy, the minus sign being a convention relative to the +lambda rise of the lift around a counterclockwise loop.
For a principal bundle with structure group G the curvature is Omega = dA + (1/2)[A ^ A]; for abelian G (e.g. U(1) or (R, +)) Omega = dA.
For a connection on a principal bundle over a connected base, the following are equivalent: Omega = 0; the horizontal distribution is integrable; every contractible loop has trivial holonomy.

On the Hopf bundle with horizontal = orthogonal to the fibres in the round metric of S^3 and the Hopf map onto the unit S^2, the holonomy of a loop on S^2 is a phase equal to half the enclosed solid angle (up to a sign convention), the Berry phase of a spin-1/2.
The non-collinear configurations in R^{3N} form the total space of a principal SE(3)-bundle over M = R^{3N}/SE(3), with rigid motions as fibres.
For the mechanical connection the translational part is flat: with zero linear momentum the centre of mass stays fixed.

The rotational part of the mechanical connection is A = I(x)^{-1} L, with L the angular momentum about the centre of mass and I(x) the locked inertia tensor, which is invertible iff the atoms are not all collinear.
For horizontal u, v at x, the curvature of the mechanical connection (rotational part) is Omega_x(u, v) = 2 I(x)^{-1} sum_i m_i u_i x v_i, up to an overall sign convention.

The film's shape coordinates are a torsion a (oxygen and hydrogen rotated by a about the C-C bond axis) and a bend b (nitrogen rotated by b about the central carbon, about the normal to the plane of the two carbons and the nitrogen), in radians.

The film's loop is (a, b)(tau) = s (1.5 cos 2 pi tau, 0.5 sin 2 pi tau), 0 <= tau <= 1, enclosing coordinate area pi * 1.5 * 0.5 * s^2, approximately 2.356 s^2 rad^2; masses are C 12, C 12, O 16, N 14, H 1.

With the shape prescribed in the body frame (positions q_i relative to the centre of mass) and zero total angular momentum, the orientation R obeys omega = -I(q)^{-1} sum_i m_i q_i x dq_i/dt and dR/dt = R [omega]_x.

Numerically (midpoint rule, 800-8000 steps, results stable in the digits shown), one loop at s = 1 returns the shape exactly and rotates the molecule by 12.50 degrees; two loops rotate it by 25.01 degrees.

The rotation accumulated over a closed loop of shapes at zero angular momentum is the holonomy of the mechanical connection; it depends only on the loop as an oriented curve in M, not on its parametrisation, and reversing the loop gives the inverse rotation.
Rotation per loop for s = 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8: 12.50, 3.09, 0.78, 0.195 degrees, with enclosed areas 2.356, 0.589, 0.147, 0.0368 rad^2 and ratios 5.31, 5.24, 5.28, 5.30 degrees per rad^2.

The ratio rotation/area settles near 5.3 degrees per rad^2, the size of the curvature of the shape-space bundle at the rest shape in the plane of the torsion and bend coordinates; the value depends on the coordinates but its being nonzero does not.

Because the curvature of the mechanical connection is nonzero at the rest shape, its horizontal distribution is not integrable: no choice of orientation for each shape (even near the rest shape) is preserved by all zero-angular-momentum motions.

In the toy cat, two rigid halves rotate about a common long axis with moments of inertia 1 (legs tucked) and 4 (legs extended); zero angular momentum about the axis reads I_front dtheta_front/dt + I_back dtheta_back/dt = 0.

With relative twist delta = theta_front - theta_back, during a twist dtheta_front/dt = I_back/(I_front + I_back) ddelta/dt and dtheta_back/dt = -I_front/(I_front + I_back) ddelta/dt; changing the legs at fixed twist turns neither half (a modelling assumption).

The toy loop (front tucked, back extended; twist 150 degrees; swap; twist back 150 degrees; relax) turns the front by +120 then -30 degrees and the back by -30 then +120 degrees: both halves turn by 90 degrees and the shape returns.
The net turn per loop of the toy cat is Delta theta = Delta delta (I_out - I_in)/(I_out + I_in) = (3/5) * 150 = 90 degrees; it is zero for equal inertias.
Two loops turn the toy cat by 180 degrees, so a cat dropped upside down lands feet first with zero angular momentum throughout and no rigid rotation of the whole body.

With w(p) = I_front/(I_front + I_back) depending on the leg pose p, the toy's constraint is A = dtheta_back + w(p) ddelta = 0, so A is a connection form on the bundle of orientations over the (delta, p) shape plane, with curvature dA = w'(p) dp ^ ddelta.

Around a closed loop gamma in the shape plane, Delta theta_back = - integral over gamma of w(p) ddelta, which by Stokes' theorem equals minus the integral of the curvature over the enclosed region; for the film's rectangle it is 150 * (4/5 - 1/5) = 90 degrees.
Kane and Scher (1969) modelled the falling cat as two rigid bodies joined at the waist; Montgomery (1993) treated the falling cat as a gauge theory on shape space.

Over a circle (the torus bundle) curvature must vanish; over the plane of tiles, over molecular shape space and over the toy cat's shape plane it does not, and nonzero curvature is what allows nontrivial holonomy around contractible loops.
